Recall which glucose polysaccharide has very frequent alpha-1,6 branch points to give many short side chains for rapid mobilisation.
walkthrough:
**Observe the shape**

Look at the diagram. You can see long chains of hexagons (glucose units) that keep splitting. There are lots of branch points, giving many short ends.

This tells you it is a highly branched polysaccharide.

**Compare the glucose polysaccharides**

Remember the key structural differences. Cellulose is straight and unbranched. Amylose is unbranched and coiled into a helix. Amylopectin (part of starch) is branched, but only every 20 to 30 glucose units. Glycogen is very highly branched, about every 8 to 12 glucose units.

**Match to the molecule**

The diagram shows extremely frequent branching with many short outer chains. That matches the structure of glycogen, the animal storage polysaccharide adapted for fast hydrolysis to release glucose.

options.A: Amylose is unbranched with only alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds and forms a helix, so it cannot show all these branch points.
options.B: Cellulose is a straight, unbranched chain of beta-glucose with hydrogen bonds between chains, not a highly branched molecule.
options.C: Glycogen is made of alpha-glucose with frequent alpha-1,4 chains and alpha-1,6 branches, giving the very bushy, highly branched shape shown.
options.D: Starch is a mixture of unbranched amylose and amylopectin, and amylopectin is much less frequently branched than the molecule shown here.
